issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette:
David, a 51-year-old school principal, had always been the person others relied on—steady, dependable, the one who held his family together after his wife’s death seven years ago. That image shattered two years ago when he was rushed to the ICU with septic shock from a perforated bowel. He spent six weeks in hospital, underwent three surgeries, and nearly died. The memory of the experience is strange: when he tries to deliberately recall what happened, the sequence remains hazy, but he cannot control the sudden, overwhelming wave of terror that washes over him without any clear image—just pure dread, often accompanied by the sensation that his body is pinned to a bed, tubes in his arms, the same rigid immobility he felt during his worst nights in the hospital. Each time that formless dread overtakes him, David becomes convinced that his only protection is to hold everything around him under tight control—which is why he now rehearses every interaction in advance and steers clear of any place that might remind him of being helpless.

He returned to work as principal the following fall, determined to resume his life, but the smells were everywhere. The antiseptic cleaner the janitor used in the corridors smelled exactly like the hospital. The alcohol-based hand sanitizer outside the cafeteria triggered the same visceral recoil. Once, during a routine fire drill, the scent of rubbing alcohol from a first‑aid kit caused his chest to tighten and his hands to go cold; he excused himself to his office and sat with his eyes closed, feeling his body re‑enact the paralysis of being in a hospital bed. These triggers have become inescapable: even scheduling a simple physical exam with his own doctor fills him with dread, so he has avoided all medical appointments for over a year.

The triggers reinforce a growing belief that he can no longer trust his own body. David is certain that his body is fundamentally unreliable, that at any moment it could betray him again without warning. He has come to see himself as an unrecognisable person—the confident leader who never flinched is gone, replaced by someone who startles at a smell, who cannot face a simple checkup. Because he is convinced he cannot rely on himself, he has started rehearsing every conversation in his head before he enters a meeting, going over possible questions and his answers, as if trying to prevent any surprise that might expose his fragility. He has also cut off contact with nearly all his friends and family; phone calls go unanswered, invitations are declined, and he eats lunch alone in his office rather than risk the cafeteria where the smell of hand sanitizer might hit him. Because he is now certain his body could betray him at any moment, he moves through his day as though every room holds a potential trigger—the faintest whiff of cleaning solution, the sound of a hospital cart on television, even the sight of a bandage on a student's hand now snags his attention and sets his heart racing.

The isolation feels safer, but it deepens his sense of being a stranger to himself. The less he engages, the more he believes he has become someone he does not recognise. That belief, in turn, makes the memories more intrusive: when he is alone in his office, the emotion without an image sweeps over him, leaving him trembling and convinced that he is still the same helpless patient. The bodily reenactment—feeling his body locked in that hospital position—comes most often when he is trying to sleep, and the difficulty deliberately recalling the event leaves him feeling that his own mind is unreliable, too.

His avoidance of medical cues has made the triggers more acute. By never stepping into a hospital or scheduling a physical, he has never given himself a chance to see that he could survive the procedure, so the fear has grown unchecked. Similarly, his habit of rehearsing conversations has made him hypervigilant to any social cue that might signal a trigger; he now scans every environment for alcohol smells or antiseptic odours before he can relax. Every rehearsal is a reminder that he cannot trust his spontaneous responses.

At school, his staff have noticed he is increasingly distant. He used to walk the halls and greet students by name; now he stays in his office with the door closed. Last month, a parent complained that he seemed abrupt and distracted during a meeting. He knows something is wrong, but he does not know how to go back to being the person he was. What brought him finally to seek help was a moment in the school parking lot: a janitor was disinfecting the lobby, and David caught the smell of hospital-grade cleaner. He froze, his body went rigid, and for a full minute he was back in that hospital bed, unable to move or speak. When he came to, he realised he could not keep living this way. He is afraid that therapy will force him to face the medical procedures he has been avoiding, but he is hoping to find a way to trust his own body again, and to recognise the man he used to be.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not explicitly describe that Negative Appraisals cause or amplify Triggers; it shows triggers reinforcing negative appraisals, but not the reverse causal direction within a single paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly describe that Negative Appraisals cause or amplify Triggers; it shows triggers reinforcing negative appraisals, but not the reverse causal direction within a single paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
